docs.title: From census records to cars on the road
docs.text:
TERP synthesises every household of the region, moves it through the housing and job markets year by year, plans each person's weekday, and simulates the resulting traffic on the road and transit networks.

Get started How it works Traffic validation map Code

docs.title: Why TERP
docs.text:
• Every person is an agent

    Households, persons, dwellings, jobs and schools are simulated individually, so results can be split by income, age, place of residence or any other attribute.

  • Deep generative population

    A conditional variational autoencoder generates households beyond the combinations seen in the sample, with PUMA and household size as conditions.

  • Land use that evolves

    Residential moves, job changes, births, deaths, marriages and car ownership update the population every year from 2016 to 2024.

  • A full weekday for everyone

    TERP-Day draws activities from survey distributions, schedules them, locates them with estimated logit models and chooses tour modes with household car allocation and joint tours.

  • Dynamic traffic

    MATSim routes every trip and shifts departure times on an OpenStreetMap network with the region's transit timetables and income-based values of time.

  • Estimated and tested, not tuned

    28 choice models estimated with Biogeme; every stage tested on data it never saw. Traffic counts play no role in estimation or calibration.

docs.title: About TERP
docs.text: TERP stands for Travel, Employment, Residence and Population, the four things it simulates, and for the Terrapins of the University of Maryland, where it is developed. It is an agent-based modelling platform that links a deep-generative synthetic population, the SILO land-use model, the TERP-Day activity model and MATSim traffic assignment for the Baltimore region and the state of Maryland.

docs.text: Component Based on What TERP adds Synthetic population Conditional variational autoencoder (Borysov et al., 2019) PUMA embedding and size conditioning, PUMA marginal loss, income within band, logical repair, zone placement, workplace assignment Land use SILO engine Residential location, car ownership, workplace and school models estimated for the region; calibration and out-of-sample test Activities ABIT engine; TASHA scheduling TERP-Day: survey distributions conditioned on the day, estimated destination, stop, outing, return-home and mode models; household car allocation; joint-tour representative Traffic MATSim OpenStreetMap network with fixed speed and capacity rules; regional transit; income-based value of time; tolls

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: ACS American Community Survey of the Census Bureau; PUMS is its Public Use Microdata Sample. ATUS American Time Use Survey. BIC Bayesian information criterion, used to choose between specifications. CVAE Conditional variational autoencoder: a neural network that learns a distribution of households conditional on   PUMA and household size and generates new households from it. Episode One activity of a person on the simulated day, with a type, start time, duration and location. GEH A statistic comparing hourly modelled and counted flows; values below 5 are a common target. Hold-out half The half of the travel-survey households not used in any estimation or calibration step. Inclusive value (logsum) The expected maximum utility of a lower-level choice, passed up to a higher-level choice. IPF, IPU Iterative proportional fitting and updating: reweighting methods of population synthesis. LODES Longitudinal Employer–Household Dynamics Origin–Destination Employment Statistics. MATSim Multi-Agent Transport Simulation, the assignment software. MSTM Maryland Statewide Transportation Model; source of the zone system and the car skims. PUMA Public Use Microdata Area, the smallest geography of the PUMS. %RMSE Root-mean-square error of modelled against counted volumes, as a percentage of the mean count. RTS The 2017/18 Regional Travel Survey of the Baltimore and Washington regions. SILO Simple Integrated Land Use Orchestrator, the land-use engine. Skim A zone-to-zone table of travel time, distance or cost. SRMSE Standardised root-mean-square error between two contingency tables. TASHA Travel Activity Scheduler for Household Agents, whose scheduling approach TERP-Day adopts. TVD Total variation distance between two distributions, in percentage points. WESML Weighted exogenous sample maximum likelihood, the estimator for choice-based samples.

docs.title: Case study: pricing the Baltimore Beltway (I-695)
docs.text:
Model version

This study was run with an earlier version of the chain (before the re-estimated models documented on this site). It shows what the platform can do; the numbers will be updated with the current models.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Who would pay a toll on I-695, who would change route or stop using the Beltway, and how would the benefits and costs be distributed across income groups?

docs.title: Designs tested
docs.text:
• Uniform tolls on the Beltway.
  • An area-based scheme.
  • An income-based discount (50 % for households under $50,000), applied person by person.
  • A fixed charge per entry, to test the mechanism.

Each design was run in MATSim with the same plans and seeds as the base, and the results were broken down by person: stayers, leavers and newcomers on the Beltway, travel time and toll paid, and consumer surplus by income decile.

docs.title: What the platform showed
docs.text:
• Beltway use is spread evenly across incomes, so a uniform toll takes a larger share of income from lower-income households: the toll is regressive.
  • Every design reduced net welfare in the tests: the users' loss in consumer surplus exceeded the toll revenue.
  • The income-based discount was the only lever that reduced the regressivity, at a cost in revenue.
  • Select-link analysis traced diverted Beltway trips to other routes, such as I-83 and arterials like MD-140.

docs.title: Outputs produced
docs.text:
• welfare and revenue tables by design and income decile;
  • maps of toll incidence by home location;
  • hourly link-volume animations;
  • diversion paths of leavers.

docs.title: 1. Pick the stage
docs.text:
Short-run responses (route and departure time) need only the assignment. Responses in destination and mode need TERP-Day with new skims; long-run responses in where people live and work need the land-use model too.

Response Stages to rerun Route, departure time MATSim Destination, mode, trip making TERP-Day → MATSim Residential and workplace location, car ownership SILO → schools → TERP-Day → MATSim

docs.title: 2. A pricing scenario in MATSim
docs.text:
1. Write a road-pricing file (MATSim roadpricing format): the links, the time windows and the amount. The base file assignment/network/roadpricing_HARB_2024.xml is an example.

  2. Run the base and the scenario with the same plans and seeds:

    python pipeline/run_chain.py --sample 0.1 --iterations 100 matsim 2024 2024 1 \
       --plans population_2024_scc.xml.gz --toll my_scheme.xml

  3. Compare executed trips (output_trips.csv.gz), link volumes (link_hours_s<N>.csv.gz) and scores (output_plans.xml.gz) between base and scenario, seed by seed.

Seeds

Run at least five seeds for base and scenario. Differences smaller than the spread across seeds are noise.

docs.title: 3. Reading results by person
docs.text: Every MATSim agent carries its household income, cars, home zone and county, so changes in travel time, toll paid and utility can be summarised by income decile or by area.

docs.title: 4. Land-use scenarios
docs.text: Edit the land-use inputs (development_*.csv for building capacity, job control totals for employment), write a properties file with landuse/run/write_properties.py, and run SILO from 2016; then rerun schools, TERP-Day and MATSim on the scenario's 2024 population.

docs.title: Comparison with standard methods
docs.text: Each stage is run against an established alternative. Every variant uses the same inputs, targets, hold-out data and measures; baselines are calibrated with the same levers; no variant is fitted to traffic counts.

docs.title: Population synthesis: CVAE against IPF, IPU and weighted sampling
docs.text:
Baselines: iterative proportional fitting with a weighted draw, iterative proportional updating (PopulationSim) and weighted sampling of the training households, all on the same training records and controls, five draws each.

  • On fit to the held-out records, the classic methods are better: IPU reaches the noise level of the held-out data on one-way distributions.
  • Reweighting methods copy whole training households, so they cannot produce a combination that is absent from the sample. The CVAE generates 62 % of the held-out combinations that the training data lack, and copies fewer households than a fresh sample shares with the training data (11 % against 22 %).

The CVAE's gain is variety beyond the sample, not closer fit to it.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Calibration is confined to three groups of land-use and workplace parameters. The calibration window is 2017–2020; the years 2021–2024 are kept for the out-of-sample test. Traffic counts play no role.

docs.title: Demographic levers
docs.text:
Five levers scale the event rates of SILO: births, marriages, divorces, the shift \(a_m\) of the moving decision and leaving the parental home. Targets come from the Census components of change and the ACS PUMS. In each round the model is run from 2016 to 2020 and every lever is updated by the damped ratio

\[ \theta^{(k+1)} = \theta^{(k)} \big(y^{\text{obs}} / y^{\text{model}}\big)^{\omega}, \]

where \(y\) are the window means of 2017–2020 and \(\omega\) is a damping exponent between 0.5 and 1.0.

Lever Model / target, final round Births 1.002 Marriages 1.000 Divorces 1.000 Moves 1.000 Leaving home 0.988

The levers are then frozen, and the model is run from 2016 to 2024 with five seeds.

docs.title: Car ownership
docs.text: The county constants of the car-ownership model are updated by the damped log-ratio of observed to modelled shares. In the final round every county × car-ownership cell is within 5 percentage points of the ACS.

docs.title: District of Columbia workplace term
docs.text: The travel survey has more Maryland workers commuting to the District than the ACS: the estimated model gives 13.1 % against 9.8 %. For application, the District workplace term is shifted by −0.387 (from 1.097 to 0.710), so that 9.82 % of Maryland-resident base-year workers work in the District, the ACS 2016–2020 share. This share is therefore not a test of the model.

docs.title: Not calibrated
docs.text:
• TERP-Day is applied without frequency factors or constant adjustments.
  • None of the other choice models is calibrated.
  • The choice-based weights of the work tour mode choice are part of its estimator.
  • The road network is not calibrated to counts.

docs.title: Common design
docs.text:
• Sample. All survey-based models are estimated on the estimation half of the travel survey; the land-use models of residential location and car ownership on ACS PUMS households.
  • Weights. The survey is stratified by home location, which every model except residential location takes as given, so these models are estimated without weights. Weights are used only where the sample is selected on the outcome: the zone level of residential location (whose outcome is the home location) and the work tour mode choice (whose sample over-represents rail commuters; weighted exogenous sample maximum likelihood).
  • Location probabilities. A survey location known by traffic zone or tract may cover several model zones; its probability is the sum of the probabilities of those zones, weighted by housing units, enrolment or jobs.
  • Choice sets. School and activity-location models use the full choice set of 1,588 zones; workplace choice the chosen zone and 99 sampled zones; the zone and dwelling levels of residential location 30 sampled alternatives.
  • Specification search. Each model is built in blocks of variables from a basic model. A block is kept when its likelihood-ratio test is significant at 5 %, it lowers the BIC and its signs are as expected; non-nested forms are compared by BIC.
  • Standard errors are robust (sandwich).
  • Software: Python Biogeme for every model of the estimation package.

docs.title: Linking logsums
docs.text:
Three logsums connect the models:

  • Mode-choice logsum of a person between two zones for a purpose, from the tour mode model; it enters the stop models as the logsum detour.
  • Non-work accessibility of a zone, the destination-choice logsum over all 1,588 zones for shopping, recreation, accompanying and other trips, weighted by trip shares (0.329, 0.279, 0.148, 0.243). It enters residential location, car ownership and workplace choice.
  • Inclusive values of the residential location levels.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: No feedback from the assignment. The land-use and activity models read fixed skims. Assigned morning-peak car times are a median 0.78 of the skim   times on which locations were chosen. Weak response to time and cost in mode choice. All time and cost coefficients are negative and significant but small. A 20 % higher car operating cost lowers   car-driver kilometres by about 0.2 % (elasticity about −0.01), below the published range; the transit-time   elasticity is about −0.2. The models reproduce current mode shares through their constants and socio-economic   terms and respond weakly to price and time. Activity frequencies do not respond to travel conditions. Frequencies, start times and durations come from survey distributions. They depend on the day's work or school   episode, not on travel time, cost or the calendar year. Activity levels of 2024. The model keeps the workplace attendance of 2017/18. More residents have a work activity than in the 2021–2024 time   use survey, and discretionary activities do not follow the fall after 2019. Moves after 2020. The calibrated move rate stays at its 2017–2020 level, while the observed rate fell after 2020. Residents only on the roads. Trucks, commercial vehicles, visitors and through traffic are not modelled. Volumes fall short of counts outside   the peaks and on roads with much freight. Correlated distance terms in the stop models. The stop models combine highly correlated distance terms (variance inflation factors up to 32), each kept because   it lowers the BIC; their individual coefficients are less precise than the fit suggests. Repeated use of the hold-out half. The hold-out half was consulted more than once in the specification search of several models, so its fit is not a   fully independent test.

docs.title: Estimation and validation strategy
docs.text:
TASHA was estimated on the 1996 Transportation Tomorrow Survey of Toronto and validated on the 2001 survey, a different year (Roorda, Miller and Habib, 2008). No regional travel diary has been collected in Baltimore and Washington since the 2017/18 Regional Travel Survey, so TERP-Day replaces the second survey year with a split of the households and with independent sources for the forecast year.

TASHA (Roorda et al., 2008) TERP-Day Estimation data Toronto travel survey, 1996 Regional Travel Survey 2017/18, estimation half (10,889 households) Verification Same survey, same households Estimation half: the model run on the observed households it was estimated on Validation Toronto travel survey, 2001 (another year) Hold-out half (10,899 households), drawn at random by home county and household size, used in no estimation or calibration step Chain test – The model run on the synthetic population, compared with the hold-out half: separates the error of the activity model from that of the population Forecast year 2001 households 2024 population of the land-use model against independent sources: ATUS 2021–24 time use, ACS 2024 commute, LODES flows Replications – Ten per test; bands show their 90 % range Measures Start time, duration by start hour, trips per chain, distance by start hour; Kolmogorov–Smirnov D and P on hourly values The same four, the same statistic; plus activities, distances and tour modes by type

Every distribution, frequency and coefficient of TERP-Day comes from the estimation half; none is adjusted to the hold-out half or to 2024 data. The hold-out half was consulted more than once during the specification search of some models, so its fit is close to, but not fully, an independent test.

docs.title: Why some comparisons are outside
docs.text:
Home-county workplace share by county (18.6 points). The model keeps 41–90 % of each county's employed residents working in their home county, against 24–72 % in LODES; the difference averages 18.6 points and is the same in the base year (17.2 points in 2016), so it does not grow during the simulation. The two measure different things: LODES counts jobs from employer records, and multi-establishment employers can report jobs at one address; the model's workplace choice is estimated on the travel survey, which records where workers go. Against the ACS, which also asks workers, the commute agrees: county-to-county flows correlate at 0.995, and the 2024 activity model sends 54.4 % of commuters to their home county or county group against 54.0 % in the ACS.

Dwelling vacancy by county (2.1 points on average). This is a weakness of the land-use model. County populations are held to the Census estimates and new dwellings follow the county building permits, so vacancy is what is left between the two. Where the residential-location model sends more households than there are dwellings, vacancy runs to zero and the county falls short of its population: Carroll (0 % vacant, 5.6 % short of the Census) and Prince George's (0 %, 2.5 % short). Where it sends fewer, vacant dwellings accumulate: Howard 10.4 % and Baltimore City 7.7 % against 2.3 % and 4.9 % in the ACS. Construction does not respond to vacancy, and prices respond too weakly to rebalance demand across counties.

Vacant share of jobs (imposed; 1.2 points on average, 4.3 points in 2021). Jobs follow the job inputs (LODES, QCEW) year by year, while employment is aligned to the ACS rate of the year before the simulated year. The vacancy is the difference, so it inherits that lag: in 2021 the model leaves 2.7 % of jobs vacant against 7.0 % in JOLTS, when openings surged after the pandemic, a surge that is in no input. By 2024 the two are close again (5.5 against 5.1 %).

docs.title: Why the car time to school is too long
docs.text: The assigned schools are 1 to 4 minutes farther than the schools of the survey students (2024: K–8 14.9 against 13.7 min, high school 17.5 against 15.7, college 34.7 against 30.3). Most of the gap is present in the base year (2016: 14.9, 16.8 and 33.0 min), and it grows slowly for high school and college as the population moves while the school inventory and its capacities stay fixed. Enrolment is an upper limit, enforced by shadow prices, so students who do not find a seat at a near school are sent to a farther one. The observed times are those of the 2017/18 survey students, so the 2024 comparison also carries seven years of change in where students live.

docs.title: Developers
docs.text:
TERP combines Python stages with three Java engines. This section documents the code: which classes and scripts TERP adds or changes, how they are wired, and how to extend them.

  • Population code

    The CVAE library and the post-processing steps.

  • SILO engine changes

    Residential location, car ownership and workplace choice in the engine.

  • TERP-Day engine

    The abm.models.maryland package: generation, destinations, mode choice.

  • MATSim runner

    RunBaltimoreToll: scoring, value of time, tolls.

  • Pipeline

    Orchestration, plans converter, skims and accessibility.

  • Estimation package

    One folder and notebook per model, with Biogeme.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Coordinate system: EPSG:26985.
  • Skims: gzipped CSV FROM,TO,VALUE.
  • Coefficients live in CSV files read by the engines; every file is written by a script from the estimation results, never by hand.
  • Unit checks compare engine utilities with Biogeme's \(X\beta\) (landuse/checks/check_*.py, activity/checks/check_engine_utilities.py).
  • Paths: each script keeps the project root in a constant at its top (ROOT or V).

docs.title: TERP-Day engine
docs.text: TERP-Day runs on the ABIT engine (msmobility/abit). Its own code is the package abm.models.maryland and the run class abm.RunAbitMarylandLos, in activity/engine/ABIT/src/main/java.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: Class Role abm.RunAbitMarylandLos entry point; args[0] = properties file; seed from -Dabit.seed abm.models.ModelSetupMaryland wires the sub-models; mode.choice.model = tour_nl selects the tour mode model abm.io.input.MarylandLosDataReader reads zones, skims, the land-use households, persons, jobs, dwellings, schools and workplaces MarylandTashaGenerator generation and scheduling from the survey distributions; outings, return home, stop relocation, tours (tasha.generation=true) MarylandDestinationChoice destination and stop logits over all zones (dest.choice.model=mnl) MarylandTourNestedModeChoice tour mode choice by segment; household stage (joint tours, car allocation) WorkAttendance daily work attendance MarylandFullModeChoice, MarylandTourModeChoice, MarylandFrequencyGenerator, MarylandStopModel, … earlier paths, kept but switched off

docs.title: What happens per household
docs.text:
Households run in parallel, each with its own random stream.

flowchart TD
  A[Joint episodes<br/>frequency, start, duration, participants, place] --> B[Each member's agenda<br/>types in precedence order]
  B --> C[Outings from the workplace]
  C --> D[Clean-up of short work and lunch-at-home episodes]
  D --> E[Chains: return-home logit]
  E --> F[Main destinations and stops: location logits]
  F --> G[Tours and tour modes]
  G --> H[Household stage: joint tours together, cars allocated]
  H --> I[Outing modes; transit leg modes]
  I --> J[activities.csv, legs.csv]

Agenda order: WB, WAHB, PW, SW, RHW, SCH, JO_REC, JO_OTH, JS, IO_REC, IO_ACC, IO_OTH, IS. A conflict is resolved by shifting the episode (up to 30 min), then shortening it (to half), then redrawing it (up to 10 times).

activity/build_parameters.py writes this set from the estimation outputs and records a checksum of every source in build_state.json.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
python activity/run_activity_model.py myrun --coef activity/parameters --seed 1 --sample 0.1 --threads 6 --xmx 13g --year 2024

This copies the coefficient set into the run folder and starts java -Dabit.seed=N -Djava.library.path=… abm.RunAbitMarylandLos <properties>.

docs.title: The notebooks
docs.text:
Every model folder has a notebook, <folder>_estimation.ipynb, that runs from the raw data to the estimates:

  1. Raw data and where to download it
  2. Data preparation steps
  3. The estimation table and its data dictionary
  4. Descriptive statistics and choice shares
  5. Correlation heatmaps and variance inflation factors of the variables in the utilities
  6. The model specification (the folder's Biogeme script, unchanged)
  7. Log-likelihood at the published coefficients
  8. Biogeme estimation
  9. Estimates in the published format, fit, comparison with the published values, correlation of the estimates
  10. Hold-out log-likelihood

Open a notebook in VS Code, select the kernel Python (biogeme) and run all cells. Switches at the top choose what is recomputed; the largest models (schools, stops, the location models) default to reading saved results, because their estimation needs more memory than a laptop has.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
cd estimation/package/SILO
./run_model.sh 04_car_ownership     # check, estimate, compare; log in 04_car_ownership/output/run_log.txt
./run_all.sh                        # all SILO models in order

docs.title: Data
docs.text: The repository holds the scripts, notebooks and published estimates of every model, but not the estimation tables: they are built from the census microdata and the travel survey by each folder's input/code scripts. Each folder's INSTRUCTIONS.pdf lists the downloads, from raw data to estimates.

docs.text:
assignment/engine/matsim-run is a Maven project on MATSim 2024.0 with the road-pricing contrib.

docs.title: Built-in settings
docs.text: Setting Value Simulation QSim 0–36 h, car as main mode, stuck time 120 s Replanning re-route 0.15, departure-time mutation 0.10 (±30 min), plan selection the rest; plan memory 5 Modes fixed from TERP-Day; ride routed on the car network; walk and bike teleported (beeline × 1.3) Transit SwissRailRaptor; search radius 4,000 m Scoring performing 0.78 utils/h; per-person marginal utility of money = 0.78 / value of time Value of time usdot: 0.5 × household income / 2,080 h, income at least $5,000 Monetary distance rate car and ride $0.075/km Activities duration bins per type; shops open 8:00–20:00 Coordinate system EPSG:26985

docs.title: Tolls
docs.text: Toll schemes are MATSim road-pricing files passed as the last argument, for example assignment/network/roadpricing_HARB_2024.xml ($3.00 per crossing of the two harbour tunnels). toll.discount.factor and toll.discount.threshold give income-based discounts.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text: File Role run_chain.py orchestrator: land-use step, activities, MATSim plans, MATSim, skims, loop activities_to_matsim.py TERP-Day output + land-use persons → MATSim plans snap_to_network.py moves activities off car links outside the connected network skims_from_matsim.py AM-peak car skims from MATSim events transit_skim.py, TransitSkim.java transit skims with SwissRailRaptor accessibility.py zone accessibility by year for the land-use models

docs.title: Bookkeeping
docs.text: Every stage writes <stage>/.done.json with its inputs, outputs, checksums, duration and settings, and is skipped next time unless --force is given. Completed stages are appended to registry.jsonl; logs go to pipeline/logs/. --dry-run prints the full command sequence.

docs.title: Plans converter
docs.text:
python pipeline/activities_to_matsim.py --activities A --legs L --pp pp_2024.csv --hh hh_2024.csv \
       --out population.xml.gz [--expansion 10] [--residents-only] [--no-gateways] [--seed 20260707]

One weekday per person; tours cut to the Baltimore region (internal, inbound, outbound); homes on residential buildings and other activities on points of interest of the matching type in the zone.

docs.title: Feedback loop
docs.text: run_chain.py loop runs land use, activities and MATSim in two-year steps from 2016 to 2026 and feeds MATSim travel times back as skims, repeating a validation year until county population changes by less than 0.5 % and zone accessibility by less than 2 % (at most three repeats).

docs.title: Adding a model
docs.text:
1. Estimate it and write its coefficients to a CSV in landuse/engine_inputs/.
  2. Read the file in a properties class and add a switch key.
  3. Implement the utility in a pure class (as ReslocRespecUtility), so the engine and a verifier share it.
  4. Add a unit check that compares engine utilities with the estimation.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
TERP runs as five stages. Each stage can be run on its own from the outputs of the previous one, or the whole chain can be driven by the pipeline.

  • Installation

    Python environments, Java 21, Maven and the three engines.

  • Repository layout

    Where each component lives.

  • Run the chain

    The commands, stage by stage.

  • Runtime and storage

    How long each stage takes and how much memory and disk it needs.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Software Version Used by Python 3.10 or later every step Java (JDK) 21 SILO, TERP-Day, MATSim Maven 3.9 or later building the Java engines Memory 32 GB or more SILO (24–28 GB heap), TERP-Day (13 GB), MATSim (32 GB)

docs.title: 1. Get the code and the terp command
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Tomal121186621/TERP.git
cd TERP
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[population,docs]"
terp --help

pip install -e . installs the terp command from your clone, so it always runs the code you have checked out.

docs.title: 2. Configure
docs.text:
cp terp.example.toml terp.toml

Set paths.workspace to the folder that holds the data and receives the runs, and the locations of the external checkouts (ABIT resources, MATSim inputs). Then check:

terp config

docs.title: 3. Estimation environment
docs.text:
python -m venv ~/.venvs/biogeme
~/.venvs/biogeme/bin/pip install biogeme==3.3.5 pandas pyarrow matplotlib ipykernel nbformat
~/.venvs/biogeme/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name biogeme --display-name "Python (biogeme)"

Set python.biogeme in terp.toml to this interpreter.

docs.title: 1. Synthetic population (2016)

terp population all            # preprocess, targets, train, generate, workplaces, export, validate
terp population base-year      # fit to ACS controls, place in zones, external workplaces, export for SILO
terp population validate

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
terp chain runs the orchestrator with resumable bookkeeping (a marker per stage, a registry of completed stages and one log per stage):

Stage Command Land-use step terp chain silo-step Y0 Y1 [--skims TAG] Activities terp chain abit Y [--skims TAG] MATSim plans terp chain matsim-pop Y [--residents-only] [--no-gateways] Assignment terp chain matsim Y NETWORK SEED [--toll FILE] [--plans FILE] Skims from MATSim terp chain skims Y [--seeds a,b] Full loop with feedback terp chain loop [--max-inner 3] Smoke test (1 % sample) terp chain test Status terp chain status

Global options: --sample --iterations --threads --xmx --silo-xmx --seed --dry-run --force.

Feedback loop

terp chain loop feeds MATSim travel times back to land use and activities in two-year steps. The results in Calibration and validation use fixed skims.

docs.title: Model design
docs.text: TERP is a chain of five components. Each component's output is the next one's input; each has its own page: Synthetic population, Land use, School location, Activities and Traffic assignment.

docs.title: Stages and what passes between them
docs.text: The TERP chain. Blue: models; grey: input data; dashed: validation data. The skims are fixed: the assignment does not feed travel times back to the land-use and activity models. Step Model Input from the previous step Output to the next step 1 Synthetic population (CVAE) Census microdata Households, persons, dwellings, jobs and workplaces of 2016 2 Land use (SILO) The 2016 base Persons, households, dwellings and jobs of every year to 2024 3 School location Students of each year The school of every student 4 Activities (TERP-Day) Population, jobs and schools of 2024 One weekday plan per person: activities, locations, times, tour modes 5 Traffic assignment (MATSim) Weekday plans Routes, departure times, link volumes, travel times

docs.title: Time line
docs.text: The base year is 2016. SILO advances the population in annual steps from 2016 to 2024; the school step runs every simulated year. The activity model and the assignment run once, for a weekday of 2024, which is the validation year.

docs.title: Study area and zone system
docs.text:
The study area is the six counties of the Baltimore region: Baltimore City and the counties of Anne Arundel, Baltimore, Carroll, Harford and Howard. It is embedded in a zone system of 1,588 zones covering Maryland, the District of Columbia and parts of Virginia, Pennsylvania, Delaware and West Virginia, so that commuting and migration across the regional boundary are represented. Land use runs with open migration among 44 counties.

Study area, major roads and the screenlines S1–S7 used in the validation. Cross: Key Bridge, closed since March 2024. Roads: OpenStreetMap.

docs.title: Level of service
docs.text:
The land-use and activity models read fixed skims:

  • Car: base-year AM-peak times of the Maryland Statewide Transportation Model (MSTM).
  • Transit: door-to-door times computed on the OpenStreetMap network with the timetables (GTFS) of the 18 operators of the network area.

The road network of the assignment (links, lanes, road classes, posted speeds) is also taken from OpenStreetMap; free speeds and capacities are derived from it by fixed rules (assignment).

docs.title: What is estimated, imposed, calibrated or assumed
docs.text:
Every component is in one of four classes.

Estimated Parameters are maximum-likelihood or empirical estimates from microdata. This covers the synthetic population, residential location, car ownership, workplace and school choice, activity generation and scheduling, destinations, stops, tour formation and tour mode choice. Imposed A quantity is set to observed data: county population and employment totals, construction, deaths, job changes, incomes and school seats. Calibrated A parameter is adjusted until a model output matches a target: the moving decision, the county constants of car ownership, the District of Columbia workplace term, the workplaces of residents of Pennsylvania, Delaware and West Virginia, and the rates of births, marriages, divorces and leaving home (calibration). Assumed A value is set without estimation or calibration: the car skims, the rules for free speeds and capacities, the partner-choice distance decay and the value of time of the assignment.

docs.title: Activities (TERP-Day)
docs.text:
At a glance

Engine TERP-Day on the ABIT engine, Java Code activity/ (coefficients, run scripts, Java source) Estimated on 2017/18 Regional Travel Survey, estimation half Models 3,946 survey distributions, 13 location and tour-formation logits, 7 mode-choice models Sensitive to Car and transit times and costs, parking, zone attributes, household composition, cars and licences Produces One weekday plan per person: activities, locations, times, modes

TERP-Day generates, schedules and locates the activity episodes of every person for one weekday and assigns their tour modes. Work and school episodes go to the job and school the person holds in the land-use model; every other episode is located by an estimated model. All distributions and parameters come from the estimation half of the travel survey, and no calibration factor is applied.

How the estimated parts of TERP-Day work together. Yellow: survey distributions; blue: estimated logit models; green: household rules; grey: inputs; red: output.

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text:
TERP-Day runs on the engine of the ABIT activity-based model of the Maryland set-up and adopts the scheduling idea of TASHA. Against the original set-up it changes the following:

Part What it does TASHA-type generation and scheduling Episodes drawn from the survey's joint distributions of frequency, start time and duration; scheduled by precedence; household joint activities Conditioning on the day Frequencies depend on whether a work or school episode is scheduled that day Licence split Shopping, recreation, accompanying and other frequencies of persons 16+ split by driving licence Joint activities by work or school Joint frequency, membership and start time depend on the members' work or school that day Pooled primary destination model One logit for four purposes with purpose scales, over all 1,588 zones Stop models Stops located by their detour and the mode-choice logsum Outings from the workplace Whether, where and by which mode Return-home model Whether a person goes home between two out-of-home episodes Re-estimated tour mode models Time and cost, paid parking, children, stops; four segments Household car allocation Overlapping car-driver tours share the household's cars Joint-tour representative Joint tours take the mode chosen by a household representative with a group-level model Transit leg modes Mode of each leg of a transit tour

docs.title: Stage 1: generation and scheduling
docs.text:
The number of episodes \(n\), the arrival time \(t\) and the duration \(\delta\) of each person and episode type are drawn from

\[ P(n \mid \tau, g, h, m, r), \qquad P(t \mid \tau, g, n, e, \sigma), \qquad P(\delta \mid \tau, g, \beta_t, n) \] Symbol Meaning \(\tau\) episode type (13, below) \(g\) person segment (10): worker with a usual workplace, working at home, without a fixed workplace; elementary, middle, high-school and post-secondary student; non-worker; retiree; child under 5 \(h\) household class (3): single person, several persons without children, with a child under 16 \(m\) whether a work or school episode is scheduled that day \(r\) number of episodes of higher precedence on the day (0, 1, 2+) \(e\) episode index (1, 2, 3+) \(\sigma\) schedule attribute \(\beta_t\) start band

Episode types, in order of scheduling precedence

Code Episode type WB Work business: a work episode away from the usual workplace WAHB Work trip of a person whose usual workplace is home PW Primary work: at the usual workplace, arriving before 15:00 SW Secondary work: at the usual workplace, arriving at 15:00 or later RHW Return home from work (for example, lunch at home) SCH School, college or daycare JO_REC, JO_OTH Joint recreation, joint other activity with household members JS Joint shopping IO_REC, IO_ACC, IO_OTH Individual recreation, accompanying (drop-off or pick-up), other errand IS Individual shopping

The 3,946 distributions are weighted relative frequencies of the estimation half; when a cell is too thin, the model falls back to a coarser cell. Start times are in 15-minute bins; durations in 5-minute bins up to two hours, then 15-minute bins. Joint episodes are generated once per household, by household composition, workers and whether members work or attend school that day.

Whether a worker has a usual workplace, works at home or has no fixed workplace is drawn from the survey shares by age band. Frequencies, start times and durations come from survey distributions and therefore do not respond to travel time or cost.

The scheduler inserts episodes into the day in precedence order, shifts and shortens them to fit, and forms home-based tours.

docs.title: Main destination of discretionary tours
docs.text:
The main activity of each discretionary tour is located from home with one multinomial logit over the 1,588 zones, for four purposes (shopping, recreation, accompanying, other errands), estimated jointly with a scale \(\mu_p\) per purpose:

\[ U_{pj} = \mu_p \Big[ \mu \ln(1 + S_j) + f_p(d_{hj}) + \beta_g\, GT_{hj} + \boldsymbol\beta^{\top}\mathbf z_j + \boldsymbol\gamma^{\top} (\ln d_{hj} \times \mathbf w_n) \Big], \qquad S_j = \text{retail}_j + \sum_c e^{\theta_c} x_{jc} \]

\(S_j\) is the size of zone \(j\) (retail jobs as base, other components with estimated log weights), \(f_p\) a piecewise-linear car distance with knots at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 km, \(GT_{hj}\) the car generalised time, \(\mathbf z_j\) zone attributes (intrazonal, CBD, retail density, land-use mix, county and state) and \(\mathbf w_n\) person, household, time-of-day and tour flags interacting with log distance. The mode-choice logsum was tested as the impedance and lost to car time for every purpose. Estimated on 14,341 tours (71 parameters).

docs.title: Stops
docs.text:
Intermediate stops are located in time order by their detour between the previous location \(a\) and the next anchor \(b\) (the main activity on the way out, home on the way back):

\[ \text{detour}_{j} = d(a,j) + d(j,b) - d(a,b), \qquad LS_j = LS(a,j) + LS(j,b) - LS(a,b) \]

where \(LS\) is the logsum of the tour mode-choice model of the stop's purpose. One model per stop purpose: shopping, recreation, accompanying and other errands.

docs.title: Other locations
docs.text: Logits of the same form locate work business (workers with a usual workplace; other persons), the work trips of persons who work at home, and school and daycare episodes of persons without a school record (one pooled model).

docs.title: Outings and returns home
docs.text:
• Outing from the workplace (binary logit): whether a work episode contains an outing, from work duration, arrival time, a CBD workplace and the home–work distance. A location logit places its first stop, and a binary logit decides whether it is walked.
  • Return home (binary logit): for every pair of consecutive out-of-home episodes, whether the person goes home in between, from the detour via home, the distance from home, the episode types, person and household variables and the time of day.

docs.title: Tour mode choice
docs.text:
The main mode of each home-based tour is chosen after its destination, timing and stops are known. Six modes (car driver as reference, car passenger, bus, train, walk, bicycle) and four segments (work, school, shopping, other):

\[ V_{nm} = \alpha_{sm} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{sm}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_n + f_{s}(T_{nm}, C_{nm}) + \lambda_{sm}\, d_n \] Segment Time and cost Structure Work Generalised cost \(GC = T + 60\,C/VOT\), with \(VOT = 0.5 \times\) hourly household income MNL, weighted to ACS commute shares (WESML) School Not significant; distance only MNL Shopping Separate time and cost (VOT $12.3/h) MNL Other Separate time and cost (VOT $41.2/h) Nested: car driver with car passenger, bus with train

\(\mathbf z_n\) holds person, household and area-type variables, the paid-parking share at the destination and whether the tour has stops; \(d_n\) is the round-trip car distance. On work tours a dollar is worth 2.96 minutes for a household with an income of $84,216. Race is not used in any choice model.

docs.title: Household stage
docs.text:
• Cars: car-driver tours whose times away from home overlap beyond the household's cars form a conflict set; the cars go to the feasible combination with the highest household utility, and a tour without a car takes its next-best mode.
  • Joint tours: a household representative (the oldest member who can drive, otherwise the oldest member) chooses the mode with a group-level model for joint shopping and for joint recreation and other tours; when the representative drives, the other members ride as car passengers.
  • Transit legs: a multinomial logit gives the mode of each leg of a transit tour (transit, walk, car passenger, car driver, bicycle).

docs.title: Output
docs.text: One weekday plan per person: the sequence of activities with their zone, start and end times, and the mode of each trip. These plans are converted to MATSim plans for the assignment (assignment).

docs.title: Traffic assignment
docs.text:
At a glance

Engine MATSim 2024 with a custom runner, Java Code assignment/ (network and transit builders, runner, validation) Network OpenStreetMap roads, 2024; GTFS transit mapped with pt2matsim Sensitive to Road capacity, speeds, tolls, transit timetables, value of time by income Produces Routes, departure times, link volumes by hour, travel times, transit boardings

The weekday plans of TERP-Day are assigned to the 2024 road and transit networks with MATSim (Multi-Agent Transport Simulation). Each agent executes its plan, and over the iterations agents re-route and shift departure times until the network loads settle.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The assignment carries the residents' own trips: every car with a tour touching the six counties, and transit riders. Trucks, commercial vehicles, visitors and through traffic are not modelled, so modelled volumes are expected to fall below traffic counts, most of all off-peak and on roads with much freight.

docs.title: Set-up
docs.text: Item Setting Sample 10 % of households Iterations 100 Replanning Re-routing; departure-time mutation (shifts of up to 30 minutes) Modes Fixed from TERP-Day Runs 5 seeds Value of time Half the hourly household income (the larger of household income and $5,000 a year, over 2,080 hours), per person Tolls Harbour tunnel tolls of 2024 Network year 2024, Key Bridge closed

docs.title: Road network
docs.text:
The network is built from OpenStreetMap: links, lanes, road classes and posted speeds.

  • Free speed: the posted speed, times 0.9 below 51 km/h. Where OpenStreetMap has no speed tag (73 % of the links), the posted speed is the MDOT SHA speed sign or the median of the same road class nearby.
  • Capacity: a value per lane by road class times the number of lanes — 1,500 veh/h for primary, 800 for secondary and 600 for tertiary and residential roads — and the bottleneck capacity of the Highway Capacity Manual on motorways and trunk roads.

No count was used to set any speed or capacity.

docs.title: Transit
docs.text: The transit schedule is built from the GTFS timetables of the region's operators with pt2matsim, mapped on the road network; buses run on the road network.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• Link volumes by hour and over the day, for comparison with counts.
  • Executed car trips and their routes, for vehicle-miles and trip lengths.
  • Transit boardings by line and mode.
  • Congested travel times by period.

The comparison with counts, screenlines and continuous counters is in validation.

docs.title: Land use
docs.text:
At a glance

Engine SILO (Simple Integrated Land Use Orchestrator), Java, with TERP's estimated models Code landuse/ (inputs, engine changes, calibration, runs) Time step One year, 2016 → 2024 Agents Households, persons, dwellings, jobs Sensitive to Car travel times and accessibility, housing prices and supply, jobs by zone, incomes, demographic rates Produces Population, dwellings and jobs of every year

The land-use stage runs on SILO (Simple Integrated Land Use Orchestrator), an open-source agent-based land-use model. It advances households, persons, dwellings and jobs in annual steps from 2016 to 2024. TERP keeps the SILO engine and replaces its behavioural models with models estimated for this region.

docs.title: What happens in a simulated year
docs.text:
1. Demography: births, deaths, marriages, divorces, leaving the parental home, ageing.
  2. Employment and jobs: jobs follow LODES by zone and type (QCEW for 2024); employment is aligned each year to the ACS rates by state, age and sex. Persons who look for a job choose among vacant jobs with the workplace model.
  3. Moving: each household decides whether to search for a new dwelling; searching households choose a county, then a zone and dwelling type, then a dwelling.
  4. Construction: new dwellings in Maryland follow the county building permits.
  5. Car ownership: households update their cars.
  6. Control totals: the population of every county is held to its synthetic 2016 population times its growth in the Census Bureau's annual county estimates.

Migration is open among 44 counties.

docs.title: Residential location
docs.text:
A moving household chooses with a three-level nested logit: county → zone × dwelling type → dwelling. The county utility is

\[ U_r = \lambda_B\, IV^{B}_r + \lambda_A\, IV^{A}_r + \boldsymbol{\beta}_r^{\top}\mathbf{x}_r , \]

where \(IV^B_r\) and \(IV^A_r\) are the inclusive values of the lower levels and \(\mathbf{x}_r\) holds the car time to the county, the previous county and its neighbours, the same state, the commute of the workers, the age of the oldest member, school learning growth and crime.

Level Sample Variables County (44) ACS PUMS movers 2014–18 Car time beyond 20 min (weaker for higher incomes), adjacency to the previous county, previous county by age, same state, commute, school learning growth, crime for households with children Zone × structure type (30 sampled) RTS households, weighted Size of the structure type in the zone, multimodal non-work accessibility by age and household size, commute, price level with income and household-size interactions, share of same-income households, dwellings per acre (with no-car and children interactions), retail jobs per km² Dwelling (30 sampled) ACS PUMS movers 2014–18 Housing-cost share of income, cost, bedroom shortfall and excess, new construction, structure-type constants by children, household size and age, with income gradients

Both inclusive-value coefficients lie in the unit interval (\(\lambda_B = 0.39\), \(\lambda_A = 0.92\)). The county level keeps its fit on movers it was not estimated on: \(\rho^2\) 0.714 in estimation, 0.721 on held-out movers and 0.704 out of time (2019–2021).

docs.title: Moving decision
docs.text:
A household decides once a year whether to search:

\[ P(\text{search}) = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + a_m \exp\big[g - g_0 - 0.982\,\ln(1 + \text{years})\big]} , \]

with \(g\) the expected gain in utility from a search, \(g_0\) the gain in the first year of tenure and years the time in the dwelling. The shift \(a_m\) is calibrated.

docs.title: Car ownership
docs.text: A multinomial logit over 0, 1, 2 and 3+ cars, estimated on 91,348 Maryland PUMS households (80 % of 2014–2018). Each alternative has its own coefficients for workers, other adults, children, the age of the oldest member and its square, piecewise log income, dwelling type and bedrooms, dwelling density and the non-work accessibility gained from a car (\(\rho^2\) 0.363; hold-out 0.358). County constants are calibrated.

docs.title: Workplace choice
docs.text:
A worker \(n\) living in zone \(h\) chooses workplace zone \(j\):

\[ V_{nj} = \mu\ln\Big(\sum_{k}e^{g_k}N_{jk}\Big) + \big(\beta_t+\boldsymbol\beta_{t}^{\top}\mathbf x_{n}\big)t_{hj} + \beta_{l}\ln(1+t_{hj}) + \beta_a A_j + \boldsymbol\beta_z^{\top}\mathbf z_{hj} + \boldsymbol\gamma^{\top}\mathbf s_{nj} \]

where \(N_{jk}\) are the jobs of type \(k\) in zone \(j\), \(t_{hj}\) the AM-peak car time with slopes that vary by person variables, \(A_j\) the non-work accessibility of the workplace zone, \(\mathbf z_{hj}\) boundary and regional terms, and \(\mathbf s_{nj}\) job-mix and wage terms interacted with person variables. Estimated on 9,707 workers with the chosen zone and 99 sampled zones (36 parameters):

  • the time slope is −0.069 per minute for the mean worker; women are 22 % more time-sensitive;
  • the preference for high-wage zones rises with income, from 0.85 below $40,000 to 3.53 at $125,000 or more;
  • hold-out log-likelihood: −4.808 per worker over all 1,587 zones with jobs.

docs.title: Other components
docs.text:
• Partner matching uses an assumed distance decay.
  • Births, marriages, divorces, leaving home use the SILO rates, scaled by calibrated factors.
  • Deaths, incomes and job changes follow the SILO engine and its inputs.

Full estimates of all land-use models are in the estimation package (see Estimation package).

docs.title: Synthetic population
docs.text:
At a glance

Engine Conditional variational autoencoder, Python and PyTorch Code population/cvae (generator), population/post (zones, dwellings, jobs, workplaces) Trained on ACS PUMS 2012–2016, 253,029 households in 96 PUMAs Produces Households, persons, dwellings, jobs and workplaces of 2016 in SILO format Runs Once, for the base year

The base population of 2016 is generated by a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) that learns the joint distribution of household and person attributes from census microdata, and then draws new households from it. Unlike reweighting methods (IPF, IPU), which can only copy households of the sample, the CVAE can generate combinations of attributes that the sample does not contain.

docs.title: Training data
docs.text:
• ACS PUMS 2012–2016 five-year sample: 253,029 households and 626,201 persons in the 96 PUMAs of the six states the zone system covers. In PUMAs only partly inside the zone system, the weights are scaled by the covered share.
  • Within each PUMA the households are split at random into training (80 %, 202,427 households), validation (10 %) and test (10 %) sets. The test set is used only for validation.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
A household is the vector \(\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{p}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{p}_7)\): four household attributes and eight attributes of each of up to seven persons, householder first. Every attribute is categorical; incomes are in bands, so the long upper tail needs no top code.

The condition \(\mathbf{c} = (\mathbf{e}_g, \mathbf{s})\) is a learned 8-dimensional embedding \(\mathbf{e}_g\) of the PUMA \(g\) and the one-hot household size \(\mathbf{s}\); the size fixes how many person slots are filled.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The conditional variational autoencoder.
  • Encoder \(q_\phi(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c})\): the one-hot household and the condition pass through two layers of 256 units (layer normalisation, GELU) to the mean and log-variance of a 24-dimensional Gaussian latent vector \(\mathbf{z}\).
  • Decoder \(p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{c})\): two layers of 256 units to a hidden state; one softmax per household attribute, and a person head shared by all slots that takes the hidden state and the slot number and gives one softmax per person attribute.

Given \(\mathbf{z}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\) the attributes are independent; their joint dependence, within the household and among its members, is carried by \(\mathbf{z}\).

docs.title: Loss
docs.text:
For a batch of households \(n\) with normalised weights \(w_n\):

\[ \mathcal{L} = \sum_n w_n \Big[ -\sum_{k} \ln p_\theta(h_{nk} \mid \mathbf{z}_n, \mathbf{c}_n) - \sum_{i=1}^{7} m_{ni} \sum_{k} \ln p_\theta(p_{nik} \mid \mathbf{z}_n, \mathbf{c}_n) \Big] + \beta \sum_{d=1}^{24} \max\big(\lambda, \overline{\mathrm{KL}}_d\big) + \gamma\, \overline{\mathrm{JSD}} \]
  • Reconstruction: cross-entropy of the household attributes \(h_{nk}\) and of the person attributes \(p_{nik}\) of the filled slots (\(m_{ni} = 1\)).
  • Kullback–Leibler term: each latent dimension is charged at least \(\lambda = 0.5\) nats (free bits), so the decoder cannot ignore the latent vector; \(\beta\) rises from 0 to 1 over the first 30 epochs.
  • Marginal term: households decoded from prior draws are summed by PUMA, and \(\overline{\mathrm{JSD}}\) is the mean Jensen–Shannon divergence between these marginals and the weighted PUMS marginals of the PUMA over twelve attributes; \(\gamma = 2\).

docs.title: Training
docs.text: AdamW (learning rate \(10^{-3}\), weight decay \(10^{-5}\)), batches of 512 households, gradients clipped to norm 1. An exponential moving average of the weights (decay 0.999) is used for generation. Training stops when the validation loss has not improved for 25 epochs; the best epoch is 197.

docs.title: Generation
docs.text:
1. For each PUMA, the household count of the PUMS weights is drawn as pairs of PUMA and size, in proportion to their weighted frequency.
  2. For each pair, \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) is decoded and every attribute is sampled from its softmax.
  3. Exact age is drawn uniformly within the five-year band; dollar incomes are drawn from the PUMS incomes of the same PUMA and band, and person incomes are rescaled to sum to the household income.
  4. Five logical rules are imposed: children under 6 have the under-6 occupation; nobody under 16 is employed, has a licence or is a spouse; nobody under 62 is retired; the first person is the only householder.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Within each PUMA the generated households are redrawn with replacement, with weights from iterative proportional fitting, so that the household count equals the ACS 2014–2018 count and persons in four age bands (0–17, 18–34, 35–64, 65+) equal the ACS household population. Household size enters with a damping exponent of 0.15, because the ACS household and person weights disagree on the mean size by about 6 %; weights are bounded to 0.2–5.

docs.title: From PUMAs to zones
docs.text: Each household is placed in a zone of its PUMA, in proportion to the zones' households: in Maryland the occupied housing units of 2016, interpolated between the 2010 and 2020 Census block counts; elsewhere the MSTM 2016 household counts. Each household receives an occupied dwelling of its generated type and tenure; bedrooms, monthly cost and year built are copied from a PUMS household of the same PUMA, type, tenure and income band. Vacant dwellings are added from the Census block counts, reduced to the share on the market.

docs.title: Employment, jobs and workplaces
docs.text:
• Employment by single year of age and sex is brought to the ACS rates that SILO uses in later years.
  • Jobs are the 2016 LODES workplace counts by zone and type (retail, office, industry, other) in Maryland and the MSTM 2016 inventory elsewhere; jobs not covered by LODES are added so that 4.01 % of jobs are vacant (JOLTS 2016).
  • The 4,960,054 workers living in Maryland, the District of Columbia and Virginia are given a workplace with the estimated workplace-choice model (landuse), with zone shadow prices updated until predicted workers equal filled jobs in every zone. Workers in Pennsylvania, Delaware and West Virginia are assigned by a doubly constrained gravity model with the ACS county-to-county commuting flows as a third constraint.

docs.title: The 2016 base
docs.text:
Item Count Households 4,704,934 Persons 12,488,143 Employed persons 6,453,136 Dwellings (vacant) 4,862,410 (157,476) Jobs (vacant) 6,722,717 (269,581)

For Maryland residents, the county-to-county commuting flows correlate with the ACS 2016–2020 flows at 0.992. The fit of the population is reported in validation.

docs.title: School location
docs.text:
At a glance

Engine Python, run after every SILO year Code landuse/schools Models Three multinomial logits: K–8, high school, college Sensitive to Car time, attendance boundaries, enrolment and capacity Produces The school of every student

Every simulated year, students are assigned to schools by three multinomial logits over the zones with enrolment of the student's band:

Band Zones Observations K–8 1,144 1,509 High school 719 668 College 141 673

Each model has a size term in which public enrolment inside the home's attendance zone is a separate component, car time and boundary terms. The attendance boundary dominates public K–12 choice: an in-boundary seat weighs about 420 times an out-of-boundary public seat in K–8 and 68 times in high school. Enrolment is an upper limit, enforced by shadow prices, and student status is aligned to the ACS enrolment rates.
